author: blu
body: Hardware abstraction layer for IoT targets. This chapter defines the configuration types and the MMIO surface. Register-level drivers live in the board chapters (Stm32F4Board, Esp32C6Board, Pi4Board, QemuVirtBoard, and five others).

author: blu
body: Touching a register is device I/O and is typed [Device.Mmio], so a driver cannot read or write hardware while claiming to be pure.

author: blu
body: Peripherals are linear resources: open them, use them, close them. The type system counts every mention of a handle, so forgetting to close one is a leak the compiler rejects (CDX2063), releasing one twice is rejected (CDX2061), and touching one after release is rejected for the same reason -- the close consumed it.

author: blu
body: So the handles are `linear`. The type system counts every mention: forgetting to close is CDX2063 (leak), closing twice is CDX2061 (double release), and using a handle after closing it is CDX2061 as well, because the close consumed it.

author: blu
body: The handle is a single-constructor variant carrying the peripheral's base address, which lets an operation destructure it (one mention), do its register access, and hand back a fresh handle. That thread-it- through shape is what keeps the resource exactly-once while still letting a caller do a sequence of writes.

author: blu
body: A bank is linear, and its lifecycle is the one the hardware demands: unlock, program, lock. An unsealed bank is not a leaked handle, it is a live write path into the running image, so dropping one is CDX2063 and sealing it twice is CDX2061.
